III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01420
We can only regret Sâ'inoddîn's reserve in referring the seeker to other, more complete works.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01421

Yet perhaps, without going beyond what we have tried to establish in this book, we can begin to glimpse what such a seeker might discover. What exactly does Sâ'inoddîn mean when he says that all these spiritual seekers have set out in the right direction, but that the fullness of meaning has nevertheless remained hidden from them? Is this really true of those who recognize in every spiritual seeker the status of nabî, and if so, why? These questions acquire their full force when we consider certain additional pages of Sâ'inoddîn's treatise dealing with the Ishrâqiyûn.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01422

As noted earlier, these are pages apparently lost from Sâ'inoddîn's text in the version preserved by our manuscript. We find them again in the great Persian encyclopedia called Dabestân-e Madhâhib (literally, “The School of Religions”), already mentioned here, which was composed in India in the seventeenth century. One of its chapters begins by simply reproducing the Mi'râj-Nâmeh, a short Persian work attributed to Avicenna, which in any case offers an Avicennian spiritual interpretation of the Prophet's heavenly ascent. After this Avicennian text, the author of the Dabestân has inserted several pages copied literally from the sections of Sâ'inoddîn's treatise dealing with the philosophers and the Ishrâqiyûn—the “theosophers of Light”—that we examined above.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01423

Finally, these pages end with a number of remarks absent from our manuscript. Their great importance is that they show how the Ishrâqiyûn explain the transfer of the title “Seal of Prophecy” to all spiritual seekers who attain the state of nabî. Here we should recall the significance of the proceedings brought against Sohrawardî by the religious scholars of Aleppo (Book II, Chapter I).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01424

What makes the matter especially interesting is that the teaching on prophecy attributed to the Ishrâqiyûn by the author of the Dabestân begins by reproducing a characteristic feature of Ismaili prophetology. In the Ismaili account, prophecy and the prophetic mission begin “in Heaven,” before the visible universe appears, with the Call (da'wat) addressed by the First Intelligence to the entire angelic pleroma. Here that call passes from one Intelligence to the next, until it reaches the Tenth, which then becomes the “Seal of Prophecy” in the pleroma. This Intelligence is none other than the “Active Intelligence” of Avicennian philosophy, identified by those philosophers with the Holy Spirit.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01425

Avicenna's theory of knowledge is thereby integrated into a philosophy of prophecy. The Active Intelligence illuminating the philosopher is the same Holy Spirit that inspires the prophets; the Angel of Knowledge is identical with the Angel of Revelation. It thus becomes possible to speak of a calling shared by philosopher and prophet, and to account for the continuity of inspiration and the persistence of the prophetic vocation.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01426

We have already observed that identifying the Active Intelligence with the Holy Spirit is not merely a theoretical construction. It is the intuitive perception of a perfectly real spiritual being, which can only be one and the same. This is in no sense a rationalization of the Holy Spirit. The Active Intelligence corresponds not to our calculating or discursive ratio, but to the Greek Nous, the spiritual intellect. Such rationalization may have occurred elsewhere. Here the movement goes in the opposite direction: the philosophers' calling is understood on the model of the prophets' calling. For in the conviction of Muslim thinkers, philosophers too receive their wisdom from the “Niche of the Lights of Prophecy” (Mishkât al-nobowwat).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01427

The author of the Dabestân accordingly reminds us that these thinkers interpreted the term “Seal of Prophecy” as an allusion to the prophetic soul's union with the Active Intelligence ('Aql fa''âl). For whoever—the Persian says har ke—attains union with this Intelligence, and participates in the state it possesses in the angelic pleroma, thereby becomes the “Seal of Prophecy.” Naturally, this cannot be an event taking place in the historical time of the external world (zamân âfâqî): the time in which events happen once and for all, the time in which the Prophet of Islam is said to have been the “Seal of Prophecy.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01428

At that level the event is irreversible, and no “repetition” is conceivable. When, therefore, the philosophers give the title “Seal of Prophecy” to every spiritual seeker who unites with the Active Intelligence, the event must occur in another kind of time. It must be a time without a closed and irreversible past, a time in which the event remains forever on the point of happening, ever able to take place “now.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01429

In short, it can only be existential time, the time of the soul (zamân anfosî, as Semnânî will call it), or the “time of the pleroma.” To apply the dates of our calendars and chronological systems to such time would plainly be absurd. We shall see, however, that not all difficulties disappear with this distinction.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01430

Certainly, the foundations of a theory of prophecy must be sought at the level of angelology, as the Ishrâqiyûn described in the Dabestân do. We have just said that, in this respect, they are giving voice to an Ismaili understanding of prophecy. The case is remarkable enough to deserve emphasis, especially since we are not at present able to explain it.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01431

Yet there is a fundamental difference. For the Ismailis, the “history” of prophecy—sacred history, or hierohistory—begins with a “prologue in Heaven”: the Call addressed by the First Intelligence, herald of prophecy, to all the Intelligences proceeding from it and to their respective angelic plenitudes.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01432

But this prologue also includes a “drama in Heaven,” from which our world and the mystery of the earthly Adam originate. That drama does not appear in the doctrine of prophecy attributed to the Ishrâqiyûn in the Dabestân.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01433

A few details will give substance to this outline. According to the Ishrâqiyûn as presented in the Dabestân, the first of the prophets, or nabîs, is the First Intelligence of the pleroma, the first of the Cherubim, also called the first spiritual Adam (Adam ma'nawî). This is the Intelligence Sohrawardî (see Book II above) names the “Nearest Light” (Nûr aqrab) to the Light of Lights. He identifies it with Bahman (Vohu-Manah), the first of the Zoroastrian Amahraspands, or Archangels, after Ohrmazd.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01434

The “Seal of Prophecy” at the level of the pleroma is the Intelligence that marks its completion and fullness: the Tenth. The philosophers call it the Active Intelligence and identify it with Gabriel, the Holy Spirit. In Sohrawardî's terminology, it is the “Angel of the human race.” The prophetic cycle, the succession of prophets on the level of the pleroma, remains in an eternal present, like an annunciation passing from Angel to Angel. One may compare the heavenly existence of the True Prophet in Jewish-Christian prophetology: Christus aeternus, the eternal Christ, manifested at Jesus' baptism.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01435

Thus prophecy has its original place, its source and true meaning, in the angelic pleroma. The recurring inspiration and prophetic gift “within souls” depend in no way upon the historical causality of the sublunar world. The event does not enter the sequence of material, visible, irreversible facts.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01436

It occurs in a “heavenly place,” the pleroma, whose eternal coming-to-be is a prophetic annunciation from Angel to Angel. The Angel who is its perfect fruit, its Seal, may bear several names—the Active Intelligence, the Holy Spirit, Gabriel, the Angel of humanity, the spiritual Adam—but the figure is one and the same. Whether we speak of the prophetic soul's union with the Active Intelligence or of the descent of the “Supreme Nâmûs,” the Angel Gabriel, upon the prophets, we are speaking of one event. To unite with the luminous Aeon who is the “Seal of Prophecy” is to share that very title, because he invests everyone united with him with his own status. In the esoteric sense, he remains the true Seal of Prophecy.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01437

But the possibility of union with him has no limit. The prophetic vocation will therefore never close; and the philosophy that explains this vocation, keeps its possibility open, and gives direct expression to it is raised, by that very fact, to the status of a “prophetic philosophy.” But is this “prophetic philosophy,” as it stands, complete? Does it contain everything essential? That is the question we shall ask alongside Sâ'inoddîn.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01438

The Dabestân, at any rate, justifies raising philosophy to this status by showing how this theosophy can account for the many people called to the state of nabî and the title of Seal of Prophecy. The Active Intelligence—the Holy Spirit, the Angel of Knowledge—is the educator of the human race. When a human being becomes its willing pupil (parwarda), allowing it to teach and spiritually nourish him, his original human condition is gradually overcome. He takes on the mode of existence of this angelic Intelligence, its “heavenly humanity.” To unite with it is to make one's own Return, one's own resurrection, to the angelic archetype of humanity, the Holy Spirit.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01439

Whoever (hâr ke!) accomplishes this Return becomes one of those nearest to it (moqarrab), its deputy or representative (qâ'im maqâm). For the Angel who is the “Seal of the Prophets” in the pleroma invests that person with his own mode of being, giving him his own name and title. That person in turn is the “Seal of the Prophets.” Even if a hundred thousand prophets were to assume this “identity” with the Active Intelligence, it would be true to say of every one of them that he is the “Seal of Prophecy”. This does not mean that prophetic inspiration passes “into the past” after them.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01440

The title names the status that each receives in the pleroma. This resurrection, this enthronement within the pleroma, is the complete esoteric meaning of the verse: “The Hour drew near, and the Moon split.” And when all this has been said, the verse remains the only way to suggest an event so extraordinary and invisible. That is why it is a symbol, not an allegory.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01441
It would be hard to push back the boundary any further or keep the door of prophetic inspiration open more boldly.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01442

Yet this is possible because the investiture that makes each nabî a “Seal of Prophecy” is not an event whose occurrence can be recorded in a chronicle of external, “objective” facts. In terms of such external history, calling this nabî a “Seal of Prophecy” makes no sense. The title has meaning only in relation to another time: the time of the Malakût, the world of the Soul. In this earthly world, these nabîs are never “of their time,” because each is his own time. Their investiture is the fullness, the Seal, of their own time—that is, the Seal of their very being. It is the fullness that makes each an Aiôn, what the Latin Avicennians called a saeculum intelligibile, an intelligible age or eternity.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01443

But literalists, by definition, can conceive of no time or history other than that of the visible events of the world below the Moon. To them, this multiplication of the “Seal” can only seem blasphemous or absurd.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01444

Unfortunately, the literalists are not the only ones to find difficulties in the “prophetic philosophy” of the Ishrâqiyûn, at least as interpreted by the author of the Dabestân. Everything happens as though we really do have a prophetic philosophy here, but one deprived of an essential part. The result is something like an imamology that does not dare—or does not wish—to speak its own name. Sâ'inoddîn's reservation is therefore easy to understand: “They sensed what was at stake, but they failed to learn from the Pillars of the Prophet's House (Asâtîn al-Bayt).”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01445

For among the Ishrâqiyûn of the Dabestân, the idea that a prophetic spiritual gift continues after the “Seal of Prophecy” is nothing other than an application of the fundamental Shiite idea of walâyat. They sought the inward, hidden meaning (bâtin) of prophecy (nobowwat) and its message. But they overlooked the fact that this inward meaning of prophecy is precisely walâyat. Without the imamate of the Twelve Imams, which exists for the sake of this inward meaning, walâyat would be left hanging in the void.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01446
Yet these thinkers do not even pronounce the word walâyat, although the esoteric dimension to which they appeal presupposes that the cycle of walâyat has succeeded the cycle of prophecy.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01447
At the risk of repeating ourselves (see Book I, Chapter VI)—for these matters are rarely explained—let us summarize the situation.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01448

First, by directing every spiritual seeker's vocation toward the state of nabî, the Ishrâqiyûn of the Dabestân seem indeed to disregard the explicit words of the Prophet of Islam, the Seal of Prophecy: “There will be no nabî after me.” Throughout the period after Muhammad, therefore, the use of the word nabî is strictly excluded. The word employed is walî, plural awliyâ: the Friends of God, those close to him.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01449

Of course, it is perfectly understood that, in terms of spiritual gifts—the divine graces actually experienced—the condition of one characterized by walâyat corresponds to that of the person called simply a nabî in the periods of the prophetic cycle before Muhammad. This simple nabî was neither a prophet sent to others (nabî morsal), still less a messenger (rasûl) commissioned to reveal a religious law (sharî'at). For this reason, post-Muhammadan walâyat is also called nobowwat bâtina: secret, inward, mystical, esoteric prophecy. Mollâ Sadrâ devoted several very substantial pages to this question in his commentary on Kolaynî's Kâfî.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01450

We can therefore observe, with Sâ'inoddîn, that because they had failed to learn “from the Pillars of the Prophet's House”—in other words, because they had not embraced Shiism openly—the Ishrâqiyûn he describes, and those discussed later in the Dabestân, lacked a doctrine of prophecy capable of securing the foundations of their theory of knowledge. It is the task of such a doctrine to distinguish the various categories of prophets: the simple nabîs, contemplatives in a sense, and the prophets sent on missions, who themselves fall into several categories. These distinctions depend on the different modes of revelation and inspiration received. It is precisely the theory of inspiration (ilhâm) that allows us to recognize the equivalence between the nabî before Muhammad and the walî after Muhammad. Apparently unable to preserve the relations among walâyat, nobowwat (prophecy), and risâlat (the mission of a messenger), these thinkers have made every spiritual seeker a nabî, without qualification.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01451

But they should have known that in every nabî, whether a simple nabî or a nabî morsal, the source of the prophetic gift was what is now called walâyat. This is precisely why walâyat is eternal, while the prophetic vocation and mission are temporary and passing. In every prophet, walâyat is his “face turned toward God,” while his prophetic work is his “face turned toward humanity,” his outward mission (ad extra). For him, walâyat remains both the point of departure and the point of return.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01452

At exceptional moments, the Prophet of Islam himself experienced this return to walâyat, withdrawing, as it were, from his mission as Messenger. These are the moments evoked in a famous hadîth: “There are moments when I am in God's company and neither an angel of the highest rank nor a prophet sent on a mission could contain what I experience.” At such moments, his own walâyat became manifest to him.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01453

Yet his mission as a prophet sent to others was not to reveal walâyat: it was to remain hidden within him. His mission concerned tanzîl, the “descent” of Revelation, and the sharî'at, the religious law. It did not concern ta'wîl, the return to hidden spiritual truth (haqîqat). That return is the manifestation of walâyat, and it takes place originally in the persons of the Twelve Imams, who together are one and the same Light.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01454

Just as walâyat is the “sun” of the prophetic mission (nobowwat) in the person of the Prophet, so the Imams' walâyat, their spiritual gift as those near to God, is solar in relation to the “lunar” walâyat of their followers, their Shiites. Here, too, we move toward the esoteric meaning of the splitting of the Moon. The Imam is thus the keystone of walâyat and of its entire cycle.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01455
Without the Imam's walâyat, it would be impossible to speak of anything like an inward, “esoteric” prophecy after the Prophet, since such prophecy is simply another name for walâyat.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01456

Hence the decisive importance of the question of the “Seal of walâyat,” which, as we have seen, Haydar Âmolî treated so masterfully. The First Imam is the “Seal of universal walâyat”: the walâyat of all the nabîs, with each of whom, until Muhammad, he had been sent secretly and invisibly. The Twelfth Imam, now in concealment, is the “Seal of Muhammadan walâyat.” For this reason it is said that the “Friends of God” belonging to the cycle of walâyat stand in relation to the Twelfth Imam, the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat, as the earlier nabîs stood in relation to the “Seal of Prophecy.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01457

With these points briefly recalled, we return to our two questions. What did Sâ'inoddîn mean when he said that the spiritual seekers—the Sufis and Ishrâqiyûn—had found the right direction, yet had not attained the full esoteric meaning of the splitting of the Moon? And, as we have also asked, is the prophetic philosophy of the Ishrâqiyûn described in the Dabestân truly complete? The foundations of the Shiite philosophy of prophecy, which we have just recalled, give us the elements of an answer.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01458

By directing every spiritual seeker toward the state of nabî, achieved when the seeker unites with the Active Intelligence or Holy Spirit, the Ishrâqiyûn of the Dabestân confront us with a dilemma. Either they know, in agreement with Shiite thinkers, that the walî of the post-Muhammadan period corresponds to the simple nabî of the earlier periods of the prophetic cycle. In that case, by retaining the term nabî while leaving the idea of walâyat unspoken, even though it is presupposed, they seem to offer a deliberately altered imamology, one that cannot or will not speak its own name.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01459

Or they have failed, “because they did not learn from the Pillars of the Prophet's House,” to recognize that in every nabî, the state and gift of prophecy derive from walâyat. The word may not have been used during the pre-Muhammadan periods of prophecy, but the reality it names certainly existed. We recalled a few lines ago the hadîth according to which the Imam was sent secretly and invisibly with each nabî, whereas with Muhammad he was sent openly.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01460

But after the “Seal of the Prophets,” how can one speak of the continuation of the prophetic vocation without giving that continuation its true name, walâyat, and explaining it through walâyat? To discuss either pre-Muhammadan nobowwat or a post-Muhammadan nobowwat without reference to walâyat and all that it means and implies is, in the end, to mutilate the philosophy of prophecy.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01461

Since nobowwat concerns the outward dimension of revelation, while walâyat concerns its inward dimension, it is impossible to direct nobowwat toward the inward without referring to walâyat, which is precisely “the esoteric dimension of prophecy.” The Avicennian philosophers and the Ishrâqiyûn have indeed developed a philosophy of prophecy by identifying the Angel of Knowledge with the Angel of Revelation and by interpreting the callings of the philosopher and the prophet as two forms of a common vocation.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01462

But by remaining silent about walâyat, they leave unanswered the question whether the Angel of ta'wîl, the Angel of spiritual interpretation, is the same as the Angel of Revelation. The full unveiling of esoteric meaning—symbolized by the splitting of the Moon—can in fact occur only through the intervention of the Imam. It is the Imam, through his solar walâyat, who reveals the hidden meaning to the initiate and makes it burst forth, just as the Angel reveals the outward message to the nabî. An angelology of knowledge must be brought to completion in an imamology of knowledge.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01463

We find this imamology of knowledge clearly indicated in Haydar Âmolî, for example where it is linked to a transcendent teaching on Adam. It draws upon hadîths and upon statements made in certain sermons, in which the Imam declares, “I am the primordial Adam” (Adam al-awwal). This primordial or metaphysical Adam (Adam al-haqîqî), the “manifestation of the Merciful One,” in whose image the earthly Adam was created, is none other than the First Intelligence, the first Archangel of the cherubic pleroma. He is the archetype of the Book (omm al-Kitâb), the “speaking Qur'an,” the “supreme Word,” the “father of Lights” (abû'l-Anwâr).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01464

All these names designate the Imam in his existence within the angelic pleroma, and in the rank that makes his Light the source of esoteric interpretation. Gabriel, the Angel of Knowledge and Revelation, is the organ—the “tongue”—of this primordial Adam, the first Angel of the pleroma.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01465

But the revealed utterance becomes nothing more than the silent Book unless the Imam in turn speaks its ta'wîl, its primordial hidden meanings. These brief indications already show how the imamology of knowledge completes the angelology of knowledge taught by our philosophers. They explain why Sâ'inoddîn could say that the philosophers had chosen the right direction, yet had not reached complete spiritual knowledge. The Hour is still approaching; it has not yet dawned. For the Hour is the Imam.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01466
We can therefore begin to appreciate the importance of the fact that several Shiite thinkers identified the Twelfth Imam with the Paraclete promised in the Gospel of John.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01467

Such are the reflections prompted by Sâ'inoddîn's densely argued treatise. We do not believe we exaggerate its importance either for understanding Iranian Avicennism or for understanding imamism—and, consequently, for understanding the relation between the two. This also reminds us how different Avicennism's fate was in the East, specifically in Iran, from its fate in the West. Avicennism has remained an essential part of Iran's spiritual history, and its tradition has survived there into our own day.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01468

At the same time, many thinkers absorbed Sohrawardî's work so thoroughly that we may speak, in their case, of an ishrâqî Avicennism shaped by Sohrawardî's philosophy of illumination. Sâ'inoddîn's treatise has drawn our attention to a shared theory of knowledge found in Avicennism, in Sohrawardî's “Oriental Theosophy,” and in an entire branch of Sufism. From this understanding of knowledge comes the idea that prophet, philosopher, and mystic share a common calling.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01469

At the heart of this prophetic philosophy we discover an imamology that does not recognize itself—or does not dare to speak its own name—but which is nevertheless presupposed as soon as one accepts that the prophetic spiritual gift continues and that it is directed toward the hidden dimension of revelation. For this orientation presupposes imamology: walâyat is, by its very nature, the esoteric dimension of prophecy.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01470
We can thus conceive of Avicennian-Sohrawardian prophetic philosophy as being directed toward its completion in the prophetic philosophy of Shiism.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01471

Since the Safavid Renaissance, a number of Iranian Shiite thinkers have written extensive commentaries on Avicenna's Shifâ, commentaries so substantial and original that they amount to independent works. Among them are that of Sayyed Ahmad 'Alawî, Mîr Dâmâd's student and son-in-law, and that of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî. Mollâ Sadrâ also produced an equally personal commentary on Sohrawardî's Book of Oriental Theosophy. When imamology dares to speak its name, it appears in the great works characteristic of Shiite thought, those of Mîr Dâmâd, Mollâ Sadrâ, Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, and others.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01472

Yet when philosophers and theosophers openly acknowledge it, imamology provokes the hostility of those Shiites whose blindness Haydar Âmolî denounced with such force and insight. It was their hostility that compelled Mollâ Sadrâ to seek refuge far from Isfahan for several years (see below, Book V, Chapter II). These are the people who, forgetting Shiism's original spiritual calling and neglecting even the hadîths of their own Imams, shut themselves within a new literalism and seek to ban philosophy and spiritual knowledge (hikmat and 'irfân). That a Haydar Âmolî, and Shiite philosophers devoted to the Imams, should have had to confront such outward-looking literalists is one of the painful aspects of what we previously examined as Shiism's “spiritual struggle” (Book I, Chapter III).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01473

Nevertheless, through philosophers such as Mîr Dâmâd and Mollâ Sadrâ, and through their students and successors down to our time, Avicennism enjoyed a remarkable flowering in Shiite Iran, sharply contrasting with its failure in the medieval Latin West. To analyze the reasons would make a fascinating and as yet unwritten chapter in comparative philosophy. We have just seen the connection between Avicennian and ishrâqî theories of knowledge and the philosophy of prophecy—which means, in Sâ'inoddîn's language, imamology, “when the approaching Hour has finally dawned.” Seen from this perspective, Mollâ Sadrâ's monumental body of work contains a trilogy that is both a testimony and a symbol: his three major commentaries on Avicenna's Shifâ, Sohrawardî's “Oriental Theosophy,” and Kolaynî's Kâfî, the great collection of Shiite hadîths. These three commentaries mark, as it were, the great streams from which Shiite thought draws nourishment.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01474

In the medieval Latin West, Avicennism failed. Its theory of knowledge rested upon angelology, and that angelology provoked alarm. Was it all too clearly perceived that, by grounding the philosopher's prophetic calling, this teaching invested the individual philosopher with an independence and authority difficult to reconcile with the Church's teaching authority? Avicenna's theory of knowledge was criticized as though it undermined the very basis of divine prerogatives, because it made the human act of knowing depend upon illumination from an Angel—the Angel of Knowledge and Revelation.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01475

By contrast, if Avicennism, whether in its original or its ishrâqî form, flourished in Iran, it was precisely because it led toward a philosophy of prophecy, in which the Angel is the intermediary through whom divine revelation reaches the prophets.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01476

It has long been recognized that Islamic prophetology reproduces an essential feature of early Jewish-Christian teaching about prophecy, in which Christology was the completion of prophetology: the idea of the Verus Propheta, the True Prophet, “hastening from prophet to prophet until he reaches his place of rest.” The success of Avicennism in Shiite Iran and its failure in the medieval Latin West thus each acquire the value of a Sign—a Sign by which to measure the distance between an early, eschatological Christology, called by historians of theology the Christology of Christos Angelos, Christ as Angel, and the historical Christology that ultimately prevailed in the definitions of the Church councils.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01477

When we say that imamology plays a role in Shiite theology analogous to the role Christology plays in Christian theology, the analogy holds only if we have in mind a Christology earlier than the one eventually adopted as official dogma. Avicennian or Avicennian-Sohrawardian theories of knowledge readily lent themselves to the formulation of a prophetic philosophy and to the idea of theophany (zohûr, tajallî), the divine manifestation that governs all imamology and Imam-centered spirituality. To precisely that extent, they could not serve a philosophy or theology of the Incarnation (tajassod) compatible with official dogma.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01478

For theophany takes place “between Heaven and Earth,” in the Malakût, the imaginal world. It is transfiguration: it lifts beings out of time's becoming and frees them from the chain of historical causation. A perfect illustration is found in the “hadîth of the White Cloud,” masterfully interpreted by Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî (see below, Book V, Chapter III). The Incarnation as understood by official dogma, on the other hand, brings God down into flesh and makes him “enter history.” Eventually some will conclude that God has died there, because everything that falls—or is made to fall—into historical time already carries death within itself.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01479

The Prophet of Islam could say, “There will be no prophet after me.” But the cycle of walâyat remains open. The Hour is still approaching: this is the meaning of Shiism. Theophany is eschatological; it is the irruption of another world into this one. By comparison, we may say that earliest Christianity was itself essentially eschatological, before yielding to the “temptation of history” and becoming historical, indeed a historical power. That is why “God is dead.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01480

But with him every idea of the approaching Hour has also died. By contrast, the Twelfth Imam has not “entered history,” and yet he is already here, invisibly present within it. This is the meaning of the ghaybat, the Great Occultation. That is why Shiism remains eschatological: for each believer, in the believer's relationship with the Imam, the Hour is always near. Sâ'inoddîn has shown us that this is what ultimately gives the Qur'anic verse about the splitting of the Moon its esoteric meaning.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01481

Yet our civilization has long known only the Moon's outward reality: the visible celestial body observed through our telescopes. The astronaut who in our own time became the first to set foot on its surface spoke words already becoming historic: “One small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.” Need we say that, for all the heroism of this “giant leap,” humanity has not advanced toward the Malakût by so much as a “small step”?
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01482

Of course, the destinies of humanity's religious and philosophical life are not decided in a single generation. Across several centuries, Avicennism may be taken as a symbol of the different destinies chosen by East and West.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01483

But how can we speak of that distinction today? The East has become “Westernized.” The word “Orient” retains its spiritual meaning only if we understand it as the Ishrâqiyûn of Iran—the “Platonists of Persia”—have understood it since Sohrawardî. This is why there may still be much to learn by comparing the fate of Avicennism in Iran with its fate in the West. It was therefore necessary to dwell on Sâ'inoddîn Torkeh Ispahânî's treatise. Its final chapter suggests that everything changes when “the Hour is approaching,” when imamology dares to speak its name. The drama of Iranian spirituality then appears to us in a light consistent with the understanding of Haydar Âmolî, who summed it up in several striking pages of one of his major works.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01484

We shall encounter another aspect of this same situation when we turn to the work of one of the greatest masters of Iranian Sufism, 'Alâoddawleh Semnânî, who lived barely a century before Sâ'inoddîn. Here too we find a highly original application of the hadîth proclaiming that the Qur'an has seven levels of hidden meaning.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01485

But unlike the anonymous Iranian author discussed earlier (Chapter II), Semnânî's genius for interpretation relates these mystical meanings not to the spiritual groups whose forms of consciousness they represent, but to the seven organs or centers in the subtle physiology of the individual's “subtle body.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01486

We shall see what amounts to a prophetic typology of these centers or organs take shape. The Ishrâqiyûn mentioned in the Dabestân grounded the common identity of the mystical philosopher's and the prophet's vocation in a theory of prophecy whose decisive event occurs in the pleroma. Its Seal is the last Angel of the pleroma, the Angel who is, for humanity, both the Angel of Knowledge and the Angel of Revelation.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01487

Here, by contrast, we shall be seeking to glimpse the identity of the latîfa jabrâ'eliya: the subtle organ named Gabriel, the “angel Gabriel of your being,” which becomes fully actual in each mystic on reaching the “Muhammad of his being.” In Semnânî's extraordinarily powerful work, Iranian Sufism pursues the effort to turn the meaning of Qur'anic Revelation inward, down to its deepest esoteric level, with the aim of a radical realization of the individual person.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01488

This process therefore brings the whole teaching about prophecy within the individual: the state of nabî, the prophetic vocation, and the missions of successive prophets are all related to the organs or centers of the subtle body. We may thus say that the essential purpose and goal of spiritual interpretation is the inward meaning of prophecy, the bâtin al-nobowwat.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01489

Yet, as the entire theosophical tradition of Shiism reminds us from its beginnings, this inward meaning of prophecy is the Imam's walâyat. Semnânî's allusions to it, however, will be discreet. Must we once again speak, in his case, of “an imamology that dares not speak its name”? In Iran, Semnânî is most often regarded as having been a Shiite, although some qualifications are necessary. What remains is that attaining the “seven prophets of your being,” as the inward meaning of prophecy, ought to mean attaining the “Imam of your being.” Perhaps the latîfa jabrâ'eliya already intimates this secret.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01490
Chapter IV The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
en-book-4-ch-4-s1
1. Semnani's Commentary on the Qur'an
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01491

The teaching that connects the seven inner meanings of the Qur'an with a mystical understanding of the human being, organized around seven subtle organs or centers (latîfa), appears to have been the personal achievement, early in the eighth Islamic century (the fourteenth century CE), of a man of extraordinary importance in the history of Iranian Sufism: 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (659–736 AH/1261–1336 CE).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01492

We have already encountered his name and thought (Book I, Chapter IV, §5) in discussing his account of different kinds of time and temporality, according to the levels of spiritual interpretation. He drew an admirable distinction between inner time—the soul's lived, existential time (zamân anfosî)—and the time of things, the objective time measured by chronology (zamân âfâqî).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01493

His life, too, is of exceptional interest, even among the remarkable and original figures of Sufism. Born into a noble family in Semnan, a town some two hundred kilometers east of present-day Tehran, he entered the service of Arghun, the Mongol ruler of Iran, as a court page at fifteen. At twenty-four, while encamped with Arghun's army outside Qazvin, he underwent a sudden and decisive spiritual crisis—much as Haydar Amoli would—which stripped him of all interest in worldly affairs. He asked to be released from service.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01494

Eventually, in Baghdad, he found the spiritual guide and master he had been seeking. He then returned to Semnan and founded an important Sufi khânaqâh, or lodge, whose memory remains alive in Iran today. His dargâh, or mausoleum, survived until quite recently, a few kilometers outside Semnan on the road from Tehran. Fragile, like so many buildings of the Mongol period, it collapsed some fifteen years ago.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01495

Semnani's writings contain enough personal references to make up a Diarium spirituale, a spiritual diary: accounts of his inner trials, of his own experiences and those of his disciples. Several belong to what we would now call “extrasensory perceptions.” They are all the more valuable psychologically because the world of Iranian Sufism is still so little known to us.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01496

Semnani wrote a considerable number of works. Only a few are accessible to us today, in relatively rare manuscripts; quite possibly many others survive unnoticed in private collections. For our purposes, one work stands out above all the rest: his commentary on the Qur'an, in which he develops a remarkably personal method of interpretation. It is usually called a tafsîr, a Qur'anic commentary, but ta'wîl would be the more accurate term. From beginning to end, it concerns itself strictly and exclusively with the inner, hidden meanings of the Qur'anic verses. It is an exemplary monument of spiritual interpretation.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01497

Unfortunately, after a prologue summarizing the author's doctrine and an interpretation of the opening sura, the Fâtiha, the commentary proper begins only with the Sura of Sinai (Sura 52). The reason is that this tafsîr—or rather this ta'wîl—was intended to continue the unfinished commentary of one of Semnani's distinguished predecessors in the same Sufi path (tarîqat), Najm al-Din Daya Razi (d. 654 AH/1256 CE). Semnani belonged to the spiritual lineage of Najm al-Din Kubra (d. 618 AH/1221 CE), the eminent shaykh of Khwarazm in Central Asia, celebrated for leading the resistance against the Mongols.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01498

Kubra gave twelfth-century Sufism a direction markedly different from that taken by the devout ascetics of Mesopotamia during Islam's early centuries. It would not be surprising if other religious influences, surviving or lying dormant in Central Asia, had also shaped Sufism there. It was in that same twelfth century, as we have seen, that Suhrawardi undertook to restore the philosophical and spiritual wisdom of ancient Iran. His teaching required anyone seeking the mystical path to acquire a solid philosophical education first: for although philosophical experience must bear fruit in mystical experience, mystical experience without that preparation risks going astray.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01499

Under influences such as those of Najm al-Din Kubra and Suhrawardi, Sufism would rise to the level of what, in the West, we call speculative mysticism, as in the school of Meister Eckhart. Its encounter with the mystical theosophy of Ibn 'Arabi (d. 1240) would come naturally, since his teaching brought back toward Iran, from the far western reaches of Islam, an esoteric wisdom that had originally come to him from the East.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01500
We can make out the broad outlines and structure of this coming together, but we remain far from understanding its details.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01501

In any event, Semnani's Tafsîr is a work of exceptional importance among mystical writings inspired by reflection on the Qur'an. It carries the inward reading of scripture to what seems the furthest conceivable point.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01502

Semnani himself understood how immense his commentary would have had to be if he had been able to treat the entire Qur'an in the same way: uncovering, step by step, its seven inner levels of meaning, not as an abstract exercise but by relating each level to the kind and degree of spiritual experience it indicates, and to the subtle organ that serves as its center and “place.” This may be a unique undertaking. It is a major witness for the comparative study of ta'wîl—spiritual interpretation across traditions—which we have long hoped to see developed, and which must take account of comparable works in Islam, Christianity, and Jewish mysticism.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
en-book-4-ch-4-s2
2. The Seven Prophets of Your Being
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01503
The prologue to Semnani's commentary tells us about his method of spiritual interpretation.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01504

But it is so brief and allusive that its statements become intelligible only when we turn to more explicit passages in his other works. From the opening lines, what strikes us is his insistence on terminology. So conscious is he of opening a new path that he urges his reader to master its technical language; otherwise, the reader will soon lose the way.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01505

Semnani himself feels bound to offer at least a short explanation, knowing that without one his commentary might become unintelligible after his death. Here the terminology also governs the entire perspective of interpretation. Semnani's sevenfold reading of the Qur'an seeks to guide us through something like a world of seven dimensions. Its guiding law is the law of correspondences, the symbolism that connects different worlds. Outer events correspond to events within the soul—that is the governing principle of spiritual interpretation itself.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01506

And the events spoken of in the divine teachings of the Book correspond to the seven organs, the seven subtle centers or regions, of mystical human nature (latâ'if insâniya). Since there are seven of these “subtle organs,” a prophet corresponds to each. In other words, every organ of the subtle human constitution embodies, within the human microcosm, the image and role of a particular prophet. Each is also marked by a colored light that the mystic can see in contemplation, and must learn to observe, for the light reveals the mystic's own spiritual condition.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01507

The first of these organs is called the subtle bodily organ, the subtle region of the bodily “mold” (latîfa qâlabîya; qâlab literally means “mold”). The human physical body, already regarded as the quintessence of Creation, is the product of a cosmic alchemy. This alchemy carries on its work as it descends through the successive planes of the universes, producing a kind of fermentation (takhmîr) that culminates in a human organism: a harmonious, well-proportioned distillation of all the influences of those worlds. This organism is the jism maj'ûl, the body “constituted” at our birth into the earthly world, a perishable mold formed by a mingling of influences from the celestial Spheres, the planets, and the Elements.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01508

But the subtle organ called latîfa qâlabîya is described as arising from influences emanating from the Sphere of Spheres and the World Soul—that is, from the Korsî and the Throne ('Arsh)—without passing through the Spheres, planets, or Elements. It is therefore not the jism maj'ûl.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01509

Indeed, it is an organ that can take shape only after the physical organism has been fully formed. This latîfa qâlabîya, the subtle bodily organ, has the form of the body but exists in a subtle state. It is, in a sense, the embryo or “mold” of a new body: the subtle body that is “acquired” (moktasab). That is why mystical anthropology calls it the “Adam of your being” (Adam wojûdî-ka).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01510

The second organ or subtle center belongs to the soul (latîfa nafsîya). Here “soul” does not mean what may also be called Rûh (Spirit), the seat of spiritual activity in general. It means the soul in its particular role of giving life to a body: the anima sensitiva, vitalis, the vital and sensitive soul, where organic and vital functions take place.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01511

For that reason it is also, within us, the “place” of unruly desires and destructive passions. For the seeker it is the very “place of trial” (dâr al-ibtilâ'), where, like Noah confronting his people, a human being confronts the contradictions of embodied, passionate existence. The subtle organ centered there is therefore the “Noah of your being” (Nûh wojûdî-ka).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01512

The third subtle organ is that of the heart (latîfa qalbîya). Within it the embryo of a mystical offspring takes shape, like a pearl within its shell. This pearl, this offspring, is none other than the subtle organ that will become the True Self, the real person (latîfa anâ'îya), which we shall meet below as the “Muhammad of your being.” The reference to spiritual offspring—to the higher Self as a child conceived within the mystic's heart—immediately explains why the subtle center of the heart, destined to give birth to that child, is called the “Abraham of your being” (Ibrâhîm wojûdî-ka).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01513

The fourth subtle organ (latîfa sirrîya) belongs to the center technically called the sirr: the “secret,” the innermost depth or higher consciousness, the threshold of consciousness beyond ordinary awareness. This is the place and organ of intimate conversation, secret communion, or confidential prayer (monâjât). It is the “Moses of your being” (Mûsâ wojûdî-ka).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01514

The fifth subtle organ (latîfa rûhîya) belongs to the spirit (Rûh, pneûma). Because of the nobility of its rank, it is entrusted with divine vice-regency (khalîfa), the task of representing the divine. It is the “David of your being” (Dâwûd wojûdî-ka).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01515

The sixth subtle organ (latîfa khafîya) belongs to the center technically called the “hidden mystery,” the innermost secret (al-khafî). Through this organ one receives the aid of the Holy Spirit (Rûh al-Qods); within the hierarchy of spiritual states, it marks entry into the state of Nabî, or prophet. This is the “Jesus of your being” ('Isâ wojûdî-ka). It announces the Name to all the other subtle centers and to the “people” of their faculties, for it is their leader. The Name it announces is the prophetic figure of the seventh subtle organ, the seal of your being. Similarly, according to the Qur'an (61:6), Jesus, the next-to-last prophet of our Cycle, announced the final Prophet: the coming of the Paraclete.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01516

Finally, the seventh subtle organ (latîfa haqqîya) belongs to the divine center of your being, the eternal seal of your person. It is the “Muhammad of your being” (Mohammad wojûdî-ka). This divine subtle center conceals the “rare Muhammadan pearl”: the subtle organ that is the True Self (latîfa anâ'îya), whose embryo began forming in the subtle center of the heart, the “Abraham of your being,” as we saw above. Here is our first example of Semnani's remarkable way of making scriptural meaning an inward reality.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01517

The point of departure is supplied by Qur'anic verses describing Muhammad's relationship to Abraham: “He follows the religion of Abraham as a pure believer (hanîf)” (4:124). “Those closest to Abraham are those who follow his faith; such is the Prophet, and such are those who believe, and God is the Friend of those who believe” (3:61). One may meditate on these verses as referring to persons who appeared “on the horizons” (fî'l-âfâq), that is, in the world's historical time.
